key_terms.meaning: One oracle call applied to a superposition Σ_x|x⟩|y⟩ acts on all inputs at once, so all f(x) exist in the state together; measurement still yields only one value.
A unitary U_f with U_f|x⟩|y⟩ = |x⟩|y ⊕ f(x)⟩; each use of U_f counts as one query.
When the target qubit is |−⟩ = (|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2, U_f gives (−1)^f(x)|x⟩|−⟩, so f(x) moves into the sign.
A factor e^(iθ) multiplying the whole state vector; it changes no measurement probability.
A phase difference between terms inside one superposition; interference turns it into an observable amplitude.
A one-query test that decides whether f:{0,1}→{0,1} is constant or balanced.
Constant: f(x) is the same for every x. Balanced: f(x)=0 for exactly half the inputs and 1 for the other half.
One query decides whether f:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1} is constant or balanced; the answer is read from the probability of measuring 0ⁿ.
For f(x) = s·x mod 2 with hidden s, the circuit returns s exactly with a single query.
Given f with f(x)=f(x⊕s) for a nonzero hidden s, find s; costs O(n) queries and a GF(2) linear solve.
The nonzero string s such that f(x)=f(x⊕s) for every x; f is two-to-one on pairs {x, x⊕s}.
The unitary on n qubits with |j⟩ → (1/√N)Σ_k e^(2πijk/N)|k⟩, where N=2ⁿ; the inverse undoes it.
Given U|ψ⟩ = e^(2πiθ)|ψ⟩, estimate θ to n bits using controlled-U powers, an inverse QFT, and measurement.
Find the least r>0 with a^r ≡ 1 (mod N), by phase estimation on the map |x⟩ → |ax mod N⟩.
Factor N by finding the order r of a random a, then computing gcd(a^(r/2) ± 1, N).
Finds one marked item in an unstructured list of N items using about (π/4)√N oracle calls.
The reflection 2|s⟩⟨s| − I about the uniform state; oracle plus diffusion rotates the state by 2θ per step.
Phase estimation applied to the Grover operator G to estimate M, the number of marked items.
Bounded-error quantum polynomial time: decision problems a quantum computer solves in polynomial time with error ≤ 1/3.
The hardest problems in NP; a polynomial-time solution to any one of them solves all of NP.

takeaways: Quantum parallelism fills a state with all values f(x), but phase kickback is what moves those values into signs that interference can later read.
Deutsch and Deutsch–Jozsa replace exponentially many classical queries with one quantum query by turning phase into a measurable amplitude.
Bernstein–Vazirani recovers a whole hidden bit string in one query; Simon needs about n queries because it must collect n−1 independent linear equations.
The quantum Fourier transform is the basis change that turns a hidden period r into sharp peaks at multiples of N/r.
Phase estimation is the reusable engine behind order finding, Shor's factoring and quantum counting.
Shor factors N in polynomial time because order finding is efficient and gcd turns a suitable order into a nontrivial factor.
Grover's speedup is quadratic, not exponential: about √N oracle calls instead of N/2.
Quantum counting reads the Grover rotation angle with phase estimation to learn how many marked items exist.
The Ω(√N) query lower bound shows Grover's algorithm is optimal up to a constant factor.
Factoring sits inside BQP, but nobody has shown that an NP-complete problem lies in BQP.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to trace circuits qubit by qubit with the state written after every gate, then state the query count and the classical post-processing that turns measurement data into the final answer.

bank.q: Explain quantum parallelism and phase kickback. Write the state of the two-qubit circuit that applies U_f to (H⊗H)|01⟩ and show where f(x) appears.
outline: Define U_f|x⟩|y⟩ = |x⟩|y⊕f(x)⟩.
Prepare data qubit in H|0⟩ and target in H|1⟩ = |−⟩.
After U_f the state is Σ_x (−1)^f(x)|x⟩|−⟩/√2, so the value sits in the sign.
Note that the two f values are present at once before measurement.
Distinguish global phase (unobservable) from relative phase (observable by interference).

bank.q: Define global phase and relative phase. Why can a relative phase be detected while a global phase cannot?
outline: Global phase multiplies the entire state vector; probabilities |amplitude|² are unchanged.
Relative phase is a difference between amplitudes of terms in one superposition.
Interference terms 2 Re(a*b) depend on that difference.
Give the example |0⟩+|1⟩ versus |0⟩−|1⟩, which are orthogonal and give different H outcomes.

bank.q: State and explain Deutsch's algorithm. Show that the final measurement of the data qubit gives 0 for a constant f and 1 for a balanced f.
outline: Promise: f:{0,1}→{0,1} is constant or balanced.
Circuit: H on both qubits, one U_f, H on the data qubit, measure.
Final amplitude of |0⟩ is (1/2)Σ_x (−1)^f(x), which is ±1 for constant and 0 for balanced.
One query beats the two classical queries needed in the worst case.
Explain why the ancilla stays in |−⟩ and can be ignored.

bank.q: Describe the Deutsch–Jozsa algorithm for n input qubits. Why does measuring 0ⁿ prove the function is constant?
outline: State the promise: constant or balanced over all 2ⁿ inputs.
Circuit: H^⊗n on |0⟩ⁿ, ancilla in |−⟩, one U_f, H^⊗n, measure.
Amplitude of |0⟩ⁿ is (1/2ⁿ)Σ_x (−1)^f(x).
Balanced makes the sum cancel exactly to 0; constant makes it ±1.
Any other outcome is impossible, so one query suffices while classically 2ⁿ⁻¹+1 queries can be needed.

bank.q: For n=2, trace the Deutsch–Jozsa circuit for f(x₁x₂)=x₁⊕x₂ and for f = 0. Give the final state and measurement outcome in each case.
outline: Start from |00⟩|1⟩, apply H^⊗2 and H to get (1/2)Σ_x|x⟩|−⟩.
Kickback: coefficients become (−1)^f(x).
For f=0 the state is unchanged; H^⊗2 returns |00⟩.
For f=x₁⊕x₂ the signs give a product state that H^⊗2 maps to |11⟩.
Conclude: 00 means constant, 11 means balanced, other answers cannot occur.

bank.q: In Bernstein–Vazirani with f(x)=s·x mod 2 and hidden s=101, trace the circuit and show the final measurement gives 101.
outline: Prepare (1/√8)Σ_x|x⟩|−⟩.
After U_f the phase is (−1)^(s·x), so the state is (1/√8)Σ_x (−1)^(s·x)|x⟩.
H^⊗3 maps this to |s⟩ exactly.
Measurement gives 101 with probability 1, in one query.
Contrast with the three classical queries a bit-by-bit probe needs.

bank.q: In Simon's algorithm with n=3, the measured equations are y₁=101, y₂=011. Find the hidden string s and explain why one more run may be needed.
outline: Each measurement gives y with y·s = 0 mod 2.
Write the two equations: s₁⊕s₃=0 and s₂⊕s₃=0.
Gives s = 000 or s = 111; the nonzero solution is s=111.
Repeat until n−1 independent equations are collected to fix s uniquely.
Query count is O(n); classical post-processing solves a GF(2) linear system.

bank.q: Write the action of the quantum Fourier transform on n qubits. Show its circuit uses Hadamards and controlled phase gates, and give the inverse used in phase estimation.
outline: Definition |j⟩ → (1/√N)Σ_k e^(2πijk/N)|k⟩ with N=2ⁿ.
Product form over qubits with controlled phase gates R_k.
Bit-reversal swap at the end.
Inverse QFT is the conjugate, applied to the ancilla register in phase estimation.
Note the classical FFT costs O(N log N); the quantum circuit uses O(n²) gates.

bank.q: Draw the phase estimation circuit and show how the first register holds an n-bit approximation of θ in U|ψ⟩ = e^(2πiθ)|ψ⟩.
outline: Ancilla in |0⟩ⁿ, target in eigenstate |ψ⟩.
Hadamards on ancilla, controlled-U^(2^j) operations write phases into ancilla.
State becomes (1/√N)Σ_k e^(2πiθk)|k⟩|ψ⟩.
Inverse QFT converts that to a peak near θ·2ⁿ.
Measurement gives n bits of θ; accuracy improves with more ancilla qubits.

bank.q: Use Shor's algorithm to factor N=15 with base a=7. Find the order, then the factors, stating every step.
outline: Powers mod 15: 7, 4, 13, 1, so r=4.
r is even, so compute a^(r/2) = 7² = 49 ≡ 4 (mod 15).
Check 4 ≢ −1 (mod 15), so the step is valid.
Conclude 15 = 3 × 5; mention the retry needed when r is odd or a^(r/2) ≡ −1.

bank.q: A list has N=2²⁰ items with exactly one marked. Estimate the number of Grover iterations and oracle calls needed, and compare with classical search.
outline: Optimal iterations ≈ (π/4)√N ≈ 0.785 × 1024 ≈ 804.
Each iteration uses one oracle call plus one diffusion step.
Classical expected checks = N/2 ≈ 524288.
So the quantum method is about 650 times fewer oracle calls, a quadratic speedup.

bank.q: Explain quantum counting. Show how phase estimation on the Grover operator gives the number of marked items M, and why this also times the search.
outline: Grover operator G has eigenvalues e^(±2iθ) with sin θ = √(M/N).
Apply phase estimation to G with t ancilla qubits.
Measured value gives θ to t bits, hence M ≈ N sin²θ.
Running the circuit also reveals the optimal iteration count, so the search can be run blindly.
Contrast with the exact-count problem, which is as hard as search.

bank.q: State the Ω(√N) lower bound for unstructured search. Why does it show Grover's algorithm cannot be improved beyond a constant factor?
outline: Any quantum algorithm needs Ω(√N) oracle calls to find a marked item.
The bound is proved by a polynomial (or hybrid) argument on the state after few queries.
Grover achieves (π/4)√N, matching the bound up to constant factors.
Consequence: the speedup is provably at most quadratic; no exponential search speedup exists for unstructured data.
Mention that structure in the data can change the bound.

bank.q: Compare Deutsch–Jozsa, Simon's algorithm, order finding and Shor's algorithm as instances of the hidden subgroup problem. Explain which group each uses and what the classical post-processing does.
outline: All four prepare a superposition, query f, apply a Fourier transform over the relevant group, and measure.
Deutsch–Jozsa uses Z₂ⁿ, where the subgroup is trivial or the whole group.
Simon uses Z₂ⁿ with the subgroup {0, s}; post-processing solves GF(2) equations.
Order finding and Shor use Z over the multiplication map x → a^x mod N; post-processing is a continued-fraction step.
Shor then adds a number-theory stage: gcd(a^(r/2)±1, N).
The unifying view explains why the same circuit pattern keeps reappearing.

bank.q: Define BQP. Explain what is known about its relation to P, PSPACE and NP, and why factoring does not prove BQP contains NP-complete problems.
outline: BQP: polynomial-time quantum computation with bounded error ≤ 1/3.
Known: P ⊆ BQP ⊆ PSPACE.
Factoring and discrete log are in BQP; they are in NP but not known to be NP-complete.
If any NP-complete problem were in BQP then NP ⊆ BQP, which is not known and widely doubted.
Grover at best gives a quadratic speedup, so it does not put NP-complete problems in BQP.

bank.q: Grover's algorithm is said to give a quadratic speedup while Shor's gives an exponential one. Justify both claims with query counts and gate costs.
outline: Classical search: Θ(N) queries; Grover: Θ(√N); lower bound Ω(√N) makes this optimal.
Best classical factoring is sub-exponential (number field sieve); Shor is polynomial in log N.
Shor's cost is dominated by modular exponentiation, still polynomial in log N.
Exponential speedup is possible only because the problem has algebraic structure, not just a black-box oracle.
State the caveat: both assume a working fault-tolerant quantum computer.

glossary.def: A state that is a weighted sum of basis states, such as (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2.
The single-qubit gate H that maps |0⟩ to (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and |1⟩ to (|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2.
The adding of amplitudes so that some outcomes grow and others cancel.
The number of oracle calls an algorithm makes, counted separately from other gates.
The transfer of a function value into the relative phase of the data register when the target is |−⟩.
A helper qubit used inside a circuit and usually measured or discarded at the end.
A gate that applies U to a target only when the control qubit is 1.
A state |ψ⟩ with U|ψ⟩ = λ|ψ⟩ for some eigenvalue λ.
The angle θ in the eigenvalue e^(2πiθ) of a unitary operator.
The unitary basis change |j⟩ → (1/√N)Σ_k e^(2πijk/N)|k⟩ with N=2ⁿ.
The adjoint of the QFT, used to read phases as bit strings in phase estimation.
A routine that measures the eigenphase of a unitary to a chosen number of bits.
The smallest r>0 such that a^r ≡ 1 (mod N); it exists when gcd(a,N)=1.
The largest positive integer dividing both inputs; computed by Euclid's algorithm in polynomial time.
A classical method that recovers the rational r from a measured phase close to a multiple of 1/r.
The general technique of boosting the amplitude of good states by repeated reflection, of which Grover is one case.
The product of the oracle reflection and the diffusion reflection, one step of the search.
The list element the oracle flags with a phase flip or a 1 output.
The reflection 2|s⟩⟨s| − I about the uniform superposition that inverts amplitudes about their mean.
Given f constant on cosets of an unknown subgroup, find that subgroup; many quantum algorithms fit this pattern.
The class of decision problems solvable in polynomial time on a quantum computer with error probability at most 1/3.
The class of decision problems whose yes answers can be checked in polynomial time given a certificate.
